verdict: Federal Realty ground out steady growth — revenue up 5% to $339M and FFO up 5.6% to $1.87 a share — as new retail leases were signed at rents 14% above the old ones on a cash basis.

segments.name: Rental income
segments.note: Rent from retailers and other tenants at Federal Realty's open-air shopping centers and mixed-use properties.

segments.name: Other property & mortgage income
segments.note: Other property income of $9.4M plus a small amount of mortgage interest income.

opex.name: Depreciation & amortization
opex.note: Depreciation of the shopping centers and other real estate — a large non-cash cost for any property owner.

otherDetail: Interest expense of $49.7M on the REIT's borrowings, partly offset by $1.1M of interest income, $0.8M of income from partnerships and a $0.5M gain on the sale of real estate (which Federal Realty counts inside operating income; it is shown here so the lines foot).
footerNote: REIT layout: the direct costs are rental expenses ($69.3M) and real estate taxes ($39.8M). Federal Realty pays no corporate income tax as a REIT — it distributes its income to shareholders instead — so the tax line is $0. Reported operating income was $116.9M including the $0.5M property-sale gain counted in other income here. Net income was $69.0M, of which $64.2M was available to common shareholders after noncontrolling interests and preferred dividends. For REITs, funds from operations (FFO) — $163.0M, or $1.87 a share — is the industry's preferred profit measure because it adds back real-estate depreciation.

takeaways.title: Re-leasing spreads are the story
takeaways.text: Federal Realty signed 117 comparable retail leases in the quarter at rents 14% higher on a cash basis (25% on a straight-line basis) than the leases they replaced — embedded growth that shows up in revenue over coming years.

takeaways.title: FFO rose 5.6% a share
takeaways.text: Nareit FFO and Core FFO were both $163.0M, or $1.87 per diluted share, and management raised full-year Core FFO guidance to $7.54–$7.58 a share.

takeaways.title: Depreciation dominates GAAP costs
takeaways.text: Depreciation and amortization of $100M is the single biggest expense line — the main reason GAAP net income ($69M) looks so much smaller than FFO ($163M) for a property owner.
